description: West African empire (c. 1235–1600) founded by Sundiata Keita after the Battle of Kirina; controlling the gold and salt trade across the Sahara, Mali's rulers including Mansa Musa (famous 1324 pilgrimage) accumulated legendary wealth, sponsored Islamic scholarship at Timbuktu and Djenné, and governed a multi-ethnic empire stretching from the Atlantic to the Niger Bend through a sophisticated provincial administration.

lifecycle_phases.description: Sundiata Keita defeats Ghana at Kirina; consolidates Manding chieftaincies into centralised empire controlling upper Niger
Mansa Musa's reign (1312–1337), pilgrimage to Mecca publicises Malian wealth; Timbuktu and Djenné become Islamic scholarly centres; territorial maximum
Succession conflicts weaken central authority; Tuareg raids from north; Mossi raids from south erode borderlands
Songhay (Songhai) Empire absorbs Timbuktu and the Niger Bend; Mali retreats to its Manding heartland around Niani

rise_factors.description: Mali controlled the trans-Saharan gold-salt exchange at its source, monopolising gold from Bambuk and Bure mines
Malian emperors' adoption of Islam integrated them into the Islamic scholarly network and legitimised governance for Muslim merchant communities
Sundiata's cavalry and infantry alliance system unified the Manding clans into a professional military force unlike earlier Ghana's informal levies

decline_factors.description: Post-Musa succession conflicts produced multiple simultaneous claimants who hired Tuareg mercenaries, draining treasury and enabling raids
Songhay Sunni Ali's conquests absorbed the Niger Bend trade cities that were Mali's primary revenue source
